lesson.title: Exam Day: Turning a Year of Statistics Into Points
lesson.summary: Converts the course's inference and design skills into concrete tactics for AP Statistics exam pacing, free-response scoring, and avoiding the errors that cost points even when the underlying statistics is correct.
lesson.body:
By this point the statistics itself is done. This last piece is about translating what you know into points under real exam constraints, limited time, a rubric that graders apply mechanically, and a set of habits that cost credit for reasons that have nothing to do with whether you actually understand the material.

On the multiple choice section, know your pacing going in and hold to it, skip and flag a genuinely uncertain question rather than stalling on it. Read stems carefully for negative phrasing, such as which of the following is not true. Pay particular attention to questions that test the scope of inference distinction between random sampling and random assignment, and the bias versus sample size distinction, both covered in this closing unit, since design-reasoning questions like these show up disproportionately and are frequently missed by students who otherwise handle the computational questions well.

On the free-response section, use the four-step process as the literal outline of your answer for any inference question, State, Plan, Do, Conclude, written as separate, clearly labeled parts, because graders award points section by section rather than for a single correct final number. Naming the procedure explicitly, for instance a two-sample t-test for a difference in means, and explicitly listing each condition with a justification tied to the specific numbers in the problem, rather than a bare conditions are met, are both worth dedicated credit, and skipping either one loses points even when the arithmetic that follows is flawless.

Guard specifically against the errors that recur most often: stating the parameter or hypotheses only in symbols with no sentence of context, asserting a condition is met instead of checking it against the problem's actual numbers, interpreting a p-value or confidence interval loosely instead of with the exact template language, treating a fail to reject conclusion as accept H0 or as proof of no difference, and, on design or investigative-task questions, blurring together what a larger sample size fixes, precision and power, with what only a better design fixes, bias and generalizability, the exact distinction this closing unit was built to drill.

The investigative task, usually the final free-response question, often reaches back across the whole course at once: a probability rule from an early unit, a sampling distribution idea, an unfamiliar procedure that has to be reasoned out from first principles rather than recognized and pattern-matched. The same four-step instinct still applies, State what is being asked, Plan an approach even if it is not a named procedure you memorized, Do the work carefully, Conclude in context, but it typically requires drawing on chance and probability rules, design principles from sampling and experiments, and inference logic together in a single question. That is exactly why the course built each unit to be reusable rather than disposable.

None of these tactics substitute for genuine understanding, they only make sure genuine understanding actually converts into a score on exam day. The deeper payoff outlasts the exam itself: reading a claim in the news, a company's write-up of an A or B test, or a public health report, and being able to tell whether the sample size, the study design, and the stated conclusion actually support what is being claimed, is the skill this entire course was built to leave you with.
